Theseus. The legendary king of Athens and one of the greatest heroes of ancient Greece. He was known for his cunning as much as his courage, a man who defeated monsters and founded kingdoms through equal measures of intellect and will.

Theseus was the son of Aegeus, the king of Athens, though some accounts claim Poseidon himself was his true father. As a young man, he gained renown by undertaking a quest that seemed impossible. The island of Crete had demanded a terrible tribute from Athens—young people sent as sacrifices to the Minotaur, a fearsome hybrid creature that was half man and half bull, imprisoned deep within a vast labyrinth constructed by the genius craftsman Daedalus.

Theseus volunteered to go to Crete among the tributes, determined to slay the monster. Upon arrival, he met Ariadne, the princess of Crete, and she fell in love with him. She gave him a ball of thread that he could attach to the labyrinth's entrance, allowing him to mark his path through the maze and find his way back out after facing the Minotaur. He descended into the depths of the labyrinth, defeated the creature in single combat, and emerged triumphant.

With Ariadne's help, he escaped Crete and returned home a hero. But his triumph soon extended far beyond slaying monsters. He united the twelve independent communities of Attica into a single political entity—the Athenian state. This act of political unification makes him Athens's founder-king, the civilizing force that transformed scattered tribes into an organized civilization.

His reputation brought him into the company of other great heroes. He sailed with Jason and the Argonauts on their quest for the Golden Fleece, and his name ranks alongside those of the greatest warriors of his age. Yet his story is not without shadow. He abandoned Ariadne on the island of Naxos after escaping Crete, an act that histories explain in different ways, and one that complicates his legend with an undercurrent of betrayal.
